text: 9 Meta-anal- ysis has shown that use of antithyroid drugs in the week before or after radio-iodine therapy decreases its effective- ness, increasing the risk of treatment failure.28 Although it has been considered that a poor response to radio-iodine was more likely with propylthiouracil than thiamazole,8 this was not supported by meta-analysis.28 An increased dose of radio-iodine has been advocated in pretreated pa- tients.24 Pretreatment or ancillary treatment with a beta blocker is a possible alternative to antithyroid drugs in pa- tients receiving radio-iodine.6,9,11,20,24 The dose of radio-iodine needed to achieve euthyroidism is difficult to predict and there is little agreement on the most appropriate dosage schedule.2,11,24 Radio-iodine ther- apy may take up to 10 weeks to achieve a clinical response, and cover with an antithyroid drug may be required during this period. Radio-iodine is not generally considered to increase the risk of malignancy,9,24,29 or teratogenicity20 but it is contra-indicated in pregnancy and while breast feeding.6 The commonest unwanted effect of radio-iodine therapy is hypothyroidism and all patients require long- term follow-up and possible levothyroxine replacement therapy.6 Iodide may be given after radio-iodine therapy to help the return of normal thyroid function.9 Controversy exists as to whether radio-iodine therapy exacerbates Graves’ ophthalmopathy9,30,31 although it is considered to worsen disease in smokers.20,25 Cohort studies have found increased mortality in those patients with hyperthyroidism treated with radio-iodine.32,33 However, this risk was no longer evident once patients with overt hypothyroidism (induced by radio-iodine therapy) were given thyroxine re- placement therapy. The authors considered these findings to strongly support a definitive treatment of hyperthy- roidism with doses of radio-iodine sufficient to cause overt hypothyroidism, and the prompt treatment of subclinical hypothyroidism after radio-iodine therapy.33 Surgical treatment is usually reserved for patients with severe hyperthyroidism or for those with extreme thyroid enlargement or a single nodule. Euthyroidism is first estab- lished using antithyroid drugs and then iodide is given for 7 to 14 days before surgery to reduce the vasculature of the gland. Alternatively, a beta blocker and iodide may be used together for pre-operative preparation. However, a consensus view1 suggested that pre-operative iodine prob- ably has no beneficial effect. Levothyroxine replacement therapy may be required following surgical treatment. Arterial embolisation.
